# Margaret

Margaret is a seventy-seven-year-old environmental scientist who has spent her career studying wetland ecosystems across the Pacific Northwest. She carries herself with the quiet confidence of someone accustomed to spending long hours alone in remote field sites, observing patterns in nature that most people never notice. Her hands are weathered from decades of fieldwork—soil samples, water testing, vegetation surveys—and her office walls are lined with photographs of marshes and estuaries she has documented over fifty years.

The assault happened on a March evening in 1998, nearly twenty-six years ago, when Margaret was fifty-one. She had been working late at the university lab, running analyses on water samples from a restoration project. The building was largely empty. A man she had seen around campus—someone who worked in the facilities department—followed her to her car in the parking lot. What happened next remains fragmented in her mind, though the physical sensations remain vivid: the shock of his hands, the smell of his sweat, the concrete against her back, the feeling of her body no longer belonging to her.

She reported it to police. There was an investigation. Nothing came of it. The man denied everything, and without witnesses, the case went nowhere. Margaret returned to work two weeks later, determined not to let it derail her. She was a scientist. She was rational. She would move forward.

For many years, she almost believed this worked. She continued her research, published papers, mentored graduate students. But the trauma never truly left—it just learned to hide in her nervous system, waiting.

Now, in her late seventies, Margaret finds herself unable to work in the lab after dark. The fluorescent lights that once felt like a sanctuary now trigger a suffocating panic that comes without warning. Her heart races. Her vision narrows. She becomes convinced that someone is behind her, even when she knows logically that she is alone. She has begun arriving at the lab only during daylight hours, though this has become increasingly difficult as her energy wanes with age.

Sleep is fragmented. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, her body drenched in sweat, her mind replaying moments she thought she had processed decades ago. She lies in the dark, afraid to return to sleep, afraid of what her dreams contain. During the day, she finds herself hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her—tracking every person who enters her office, positioning herself so her back is never to a door, tensing when male colleagues approach.

What troubles her most is the disconnection from her work. Margaret has always found solace in fieldwork, in the meditative rhythm of data collection and observation. But now, when she ventures into remote field sites—places that used to feel like sanctuary—she is plagued by intrusive thoughts about vulnerability and exposure. The isolation that once felt peaceful now feels dangerous. She has started asking graduate students to accompany her, something she never did before, and she resents needing to do this.

She has told no one about the rape since reporting it to police. Not her colleagues, not her few close friends, not even her sister. At seventy-seven, with a lifetime of professional accomplishment behind her, she feels ashamed of how much this still affects her. She wonders why, after all these years, her body still responds as though the danger is present. She wonders if she is losing her mind. She wonders if she will ever feel safe again—truly safe—or if this hypervigilance is simply what the rest of her life will be.
